definition: Kudos means praise and public credit given for a specific achievement.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word kudos. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know kudos should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The kudos for rescuing the payroll system landed on Tessa all week — sticky notes from accounting, a shout-out in the all-staff email, and a cake with a spreadsheet iced on top.
A compliment is milder and smaller than kudos: one person's kind remark, offered once. Kudos is bigger and more public — credit announced to the room, pinned to something actually pulled off.
Renown is stronger and further-reaching than kudos: kudos is applause for one achievement and fades with the week, while renown is recognition that has spread far and settled in to stay.

Recognition is the acknowledgment itself — your work was seen — and it can be as dry as a line on a certificate. Kudos is recognition with warmth on it: praise offered openly, usually by name and with a little applause in the voice.

The trail from kydos ends where it begins: no other English word grew from it. The word's one drama is grammatical — kudos is singular, like glory, so 'a kudo' is a back-formation error invented by ears that heard a plural where there never was one. Style guides have been swatting it away for a century.
Kudos means praise and public credit given for a specific achievement.
After the block's power came back in record time, kudos went where it was due: to the retired lineman who had walked the crews straight to the one burned splice everyone else had missed.
Kudos is credit made public — praise pinned to a particular achievement and a particular name.
Notice it goes to the person who did the thing, for the thing: the splice was found, so the lineman gets the kudos.
Vague good vibes aimed at everyone are not kudos; the word wants a name and a feat.
Kudos sits in the friendly middle of the praise register: warmer than recognition, lighter than its unit-mates plaudits and accolade, and perfectly at home in an email subject line.
Two cautions earn their keep.
Kudos is singular — kudos is due, never 'a kudo' — and it needs a feat: the word attaches to something done.
For applause in print and ceremony, reach for plaudits or accolade; when the credit is quick, warm, and by name, kudos is the word.
